title: The Strangest Siege of the Middle Ages | The Long Footnote
creator: The Long Footnote
description:
In 1346 the besiegers of Caffa did something nobody has quite managed to prove or disprove since. Owen and Bea dig through the sources.

The Long Footnote is listener-supported. Members get ad-free episodes a week early and the monthly Q&A: patreon.com/thelongfootnote or the Join button here on YouTube.

Sources in the pinned comment.

sentences.t: Welcome to The Long Footnote, I'm Owen, and with me as always is Bea.
Hello, and today Owen has promised me a siege that is genuinely weirder than all the other sieges.
I have, and I stand by it, it's Caffa, in thirteen forty six, on the Black Sea.
Before we get into it, quick bit of housekeeping, because this is the time of year we do this.
This show is entirely listener supported, there are no ads in it, and that's because of the people on our Patreon.
If you join, you get every episode a week early, with no housekeeping like this bit, and a monthly live Q and A with the two of us.
You can join at patreon dot com slash the long footnote, or with the join button right here on YouTube, it's the same membership.
And to everyone who already does, honestly, thank you, you're the reason Bea can afford all those library fines.
That is slander and also completely true.
Okay, Caffa, so, it's a Genoese trading port in Crimea, and it's being besieged by the army of the Golden Horde.
And this siege has been going on, on and off, for a couple of years at this point.
Right, and the besiegers are not doing well, because something is spreading through their camp.
Which is, and I want to be careful here, very probably the plague, the Black Death, right at the start of its run west.
So here's the famous part, and the reason this siege ends up in every textbook.
There's a lawyer called Gabriele de' Mussi who writes that the besiegers loaded the bodies of their dead into their trebuchets.
And threw them over the walls into the city.
Which is horrifying, and is also often called the first biological warfare in history.
Okay, but here's my problem, and you knew I'd have one.
De' Mussi probably wasn't there, Bea, he was writing from Piacenza, in Italy, very far away.
So he's working from what traders told him, which is basically medieval hearsay.
Exactly, and historians have argued for decades about whether the bodies thing even happened.
And even if it did, plague mostly spreads through fleas on rats, not from bodies, so would it even have worked?
Probably not the way he describes it, the rats in the city were going to get it with or without catapults.
So the story might be true and also not the actual reason the city got sick.
Which is my favorite kind of history, honestly, a real event wrapped in a better story.
And then the part that matters most, which is what happens next.
Genoese ships leave Caffa and sail home, stopping at ports along the way, Constantinople, Sicily, and on to Italy.
And within a couple of years, something like a third of Europe is dead.
So whether or not anyone threw anything over a wall, Caffa ends up being one of the doors the plague came through.
That's grim, Owen, you promised me weird, not grim.
It's both, it's always both on this show, that's the brand.
Next week, something lighter, I promise, it's the time a French king got stuck in a tree.
That's not true, is it?
You'll have to come back and find out, thanks for listening, everybody.
